entities.summary:
Batis, the resolute eunuch commander of the strategically vital city of Gaza, achieved historical prominence through his defiant resistance against Alexander the Great in 332 BCE. During an era defined by imperial expansion and military conquest, Batis's defense of Gaza against the Macedonian juggernaut underscored the fierce opposition Alexander sometimes faced, even as it ultimately highlighted the conqueror's brutal determination. His stand, though ultimately futile, briefly delayed Alexander's march into Egypt and became a stark example of the high cost of defying the Macedonian king.

Following Alexander's victorious, though costly, Siege of Tyre, Batis meticulously prepared Gaza for an even more formidable defense. He fortified the city, situated atop a substantial mound, and stocked it with provisions, believing its natural defenses and his Persian garrison could withstand any assault. Alexander arrived in late 332 BCE, initiating a two-month siege. Macedonian engineers constructed a massive earthen ramp, 250 feet high and a quarter-mile wide, to bring siege engines within range of Gaza’s formidable walls. Batis’s forces launched several desperate sallies, inflicting casualties on the besiegers, but ultimately, the city fell. Alexander, reportedly enraged by the prolonged resistance and Batis's personal defiance, subjected the commander to a gruesome death, reminiscent of Achilles' treatment of Hector: Batis was allegedly dragged alive around the city walls by a chariot.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Batis's determined defense of Gaza, though ultimately unsuccessful, significantly delayed Alexander the Great's advance into Egypt, demonstrating the fierce resistance faced by the Macedonian conqueror. His brutal execution also served as a powerful, chilling example of Alexander's treatment of defiant adversaries, shaping future responses to his campaigns.
